# Simultaneous exposed-vertex trims and their finite incidence dual

This note extends `candidate c9f582e034f0948d` from
one local deletion to disjoint vertex deletions with prescribed removed
masses. The underlying exact quantile covers and general first-order
inverse condition are already proved in
`candidate a0fdd477aa859374`; the smooth second-order formulas are
already in `candidate a0a4e151af2d0678`. They are not
claimed anew. The additional mechanism here is a realizable probability
distribution of vertex deletions, its finite incidence game and separation
dual, and an exact case where every single-point trim fails but simultaneous
trims succeed.

The result is a necessary variational condition, not a proof that a
below-target family has a profitable trim distribution.

## 1. Setting and the actual mass-parameterized deformation

Let P be a finite base set. Let K_p be full-dimensional d-polytopes,
d>=1, which are the actual p-sections of the compact convex polytope

    C=conv union_(p in P) ({p}×K_p).

Write mu=sum_p vol_d, M=mu(C), beta for the full maximum normalized
closed-halfspace depth, and Q=beta M. Let I be its finite nonempty set of
deepest bases. All ambient halfspaces, including oblique ones, remain in
the depth definition.

Choose distinct exposed vertices v in a nonempty finite set V of vertices
of C. Each v belongs to one measured fiber, say K_(p_v). Indeed an extreme
point of the convex hull of a finite union of compact convex sets belongs
to one member; otherwise a finite convex representation contradicts
extremality. It is a vertex of that member as well. Choose one ambient
linear functional ell_v uniquely maximized at v, with maximum h_v.

Its continuous part is nonzero because the fiber has interior. Every other
base has a strict support gap. In the v-fiber, let W_v be the tangent cone
at v after continuous translation to zero, and put

    B_v={w in W_v: −(ell_v)_cont(w)<=1},   a_v=|B_v|>0.

Strict exposure makes B_v bounded: the functional is strictly negative on
every nonzero cone ray. For sufficiently small t>0, the part removed from
the actual source by ell_v>h_v−t is, up to null boundary, exactly

    {p_v}×(v_cont+t B_v),                                (1)

of mass a_v t^d. Incident fiber facets define W_v; nonincident facets and
the finitely many other fibers have fixed positive gaps. This proves (1).

Fix a probability vector lambda=(lambda_v) on V. For epsilon>0 set

    t_v(epsilon)=(epsilon lambda_v/a_v)^(1/d)

when lambda_v>0, and impose no cut when lambda_v=0. Define

    C_epsilon=C intersect
       intersection_(lambda_v>0){ell_v<=h_v−t_v(epsilon)}. (2)

For sufficiently small epsilon the original removed caps are pairwise
disjoint, since each is in a shrinking neighborhood of its distinct
vertex. Thus the removed set is exactly their disjoint union and

    mu(C_epsilon)=M−epsilon.                             (3)

No approximation replaces these prescribed masses. The cutoff can be
chosen uniformly over lambda in the probability simplex because
t_v<= (epsilon/a_v)^(1/d). Every fiber remains positive and converges
back to its original fiber; an interior ball in each fiber survives.
The deformed fibers are sections of the one body (2), so all compatibility
conditions hold exactly. This includes distinct selected vertices in the
same fiber. Nothing is convexified after making independent fiber changes.

These are admissible competitors for an unrestricted attained local
minimum on P. A minimum restricted to at most N shared planes permits
them only when the cuts remain within that class; adding new planes must
not be silently allowed at the N-plane minimum. The unrestricted attained
reduction is Sections 4--8 of
`candidate c280bb0dcfd30f3d`.

## 2. Critical caps and the deletion-incidence matrix

Choose ANY one positive critical circuit C_p for each p in I. Its caps are

    H_j={v_j.q+u_j.x>=b_j}, |u_j|=1,
    mu(H_j)=Q,   sum_j rho_j u_j=0, rho_j>0,

through one interior maximizing point of the anchor fiber. The circuits
exist by the previously proved exact critical-cap lemmas. At a base p their
weighted margins sum to zero at EVERY continuous x, so they cover
{p}×R^d. Threshold changes with sum_j rho_j delta b_j=0 preserve that
whole-fiber cover exactly; thus no choice or motion of a maximizing center
is needed in this argument. Nondeep bases retain slack circuit covers.

For each cap and chosen vertex define its fixed local deletion incidence

    iota_(j,v)=1 or 0 if v is strictly inside or outside H_j;
    iota_(j,v)=|B_v intersect {u_j.w>=0}|/a_v
                                      if v lies on its boundary. (4)

For all sufficiently small epsilon, the removed cap mass is EXACTLY

    mu((C\C_epsilon) intersect H_j)
                      =epsilon sum_v lambda_v iota_(j,v).       (5)

At a boundary-passing cap, the integer coordinate is constant on the
deleted fiber and the cone rescaling gives (4) exactly. At other vertices
the fixed strict cap-margin gap gives eventual constant incidence.

For d>=2 the interaction with any O(epsilon) threshold motion is uniformly
o(epsilon). A width-A epsilon slab meets the v-piece in volume at most

    const * epsilon * t_v^(d−1).

This follows by projecting that piece onto the continuous cap hyperplane;
its diameter is O(t_v). Summing the finitely many vertices bounds the
interaction by const * epsilon^(2−1/d), uniformly for lambda in its compact
probability simplex. In particular caps through a trimmed vertex have NOT
been replaced by open caps or assigned an arbitrary boundary incidence.

The following sections first assume d>=2. Section 6 records the exact
dimension-one rule.

## 3. Complete nonsmooth deletion test

Let S_j^+ and S_j^- be the actual positive right and left threshold slopes
of the original cap mass. Explicitly, S_j^+ is the sum of proper section
areas plus supporting-facet areas in fibers inside the cap; S_j^- uses
proper sections plus supporting-facet areas in fibers outside the cap.
The anchor's proper section makes both positive. With unit continuous
normal,

    F_j(b_j+s)=Q−S_j^+s+o(|s|) for s>0,
    F_j(b_j+s)=Q−S_j^-s+o(|s|) for s<0.                  (6)

The preceding note proves these formulas, including lower-dimensional
support faces and closed supporting facets. Put

    iota_j(lambda)=sum_v lambda_v iota_(j,v),
    Phi_p(lambda)=sum_(j in C_p) rho_j [
       (beta−iota_j(lambda))_+/S_j^+
        −(iota_j(lambda)−beta)_+/S_j^- ].                (7)

**Nonsmooth criterion.** If a probability vector lambda satisfies
Phi_p(lambda)<0 for EVERY p in I, then (2) strictly lowers the full maximum
depth for all sufficiently small positive epsilon.

To prove this, form for each cap its nearby exact quantile of mass
Q−beta epsilon. The unchanged anchor ball supplies a positive lower
section bound, so this quantile is unique and differs from b_j by
O(epsilon). Equations (5), (6), and the interaction estimate give its
threshold change divided by epsilon as

    (beta−iota_j(lambda))_+/S_j^+
      −(iota_j(lambda)−beta)_+/S_j^- +o(1).

Its circuit's weighted sum is epsilon Phi_p(lambda)+o(epsilon), hence
strictly negative. By continuity, the common cap mass can be lowered a
little below Q−beta epsilon while maintaining a closed whole-fiber cover.
The finitely many nondeep covers retain their strict original slack.
Consequently every candidate in every actual new fiber is in a cap of
mass strictly below beta(M−epsilon). This proves the criterion.

The functions Phi_p are continuous piecewise affine on the probability
simplex. Their feasibility can be examined on the finitely many cells
cut out by iota_j(lambda)=beta. A simple linear minimax dual is not asserted
for unequal S_j^+,S_j^-: these piecewise functions need not be convex or
concave with the needed common orientation.

## 4. Finite incidence game and exact separation dual

Suppose the selected caps have equal one-sided threshold slopes
S_j^+=S_j^-=S_j. For example, all their relevant cuts may be transverse.
No smoothness in the plane-offset parameter is required. Define

    kappa_j=(rho_j/S_j)/sum_(l in C_p)(rho_l/S_l),
    A_(p,v)=sum_(j in C_p) kappa_j iota_(j,v).             (8)

Thus 0<=A_(p,v)<=1. This is the simultaneous vertex-incidence matrix for
the selected original ambient caps and the selected exposing functionals.
Let k=|I| and define the attained finite game value

    tau=max_(lambda>=0, sum lambda=1)
                   min_(p in I) sum_v A_(p,v)lambda_v.   (9)

Compactness of the finite probability simplex and continuity prove
attainment. Equation (7) immediately says tau>beta gives strict descent.
More precisely an optimizer lambda yields

    limsup_(epsilon down to0)
       [D(C_epsilon intersect(P×R^d))−beta]/epsilon
                                  <=−(tau−beta)/M.       (10)

Here is a direct verification without differentiating an actual maximum.
Put a_p=sum_v A_(p,v)lambda_v and shift the jth threshold in C_p by

    epsilon [a_p−iota_j(lambda)]/S_j.

Its circuit-weighted sum is exactly zero. Every cap in that circuit has
mass Q−epsilon a_p+o(epsilon) by (5)--(6). These finite exact covers
therefore bound the full maximum by
[Q−epsilon min_p a_p+o(epsilon)]/(M−epsilon), which is (10).

**Dual theorem.** There is no profitable probability distribution for this
selected matrix, meaning tau<=beta, if and only if there is a probability
vector pi on the deepest bases such that

    sum_p pi_p A_(p,v)<=beta for EVERY v in V.             (11)

Proof: let X be the convex hull of the columns A_(.,v) in R^k. It is
compact and convex. The assertion tau<=beta says X is disjoint from the
open convex orthant {x:x_p>beta for all p}. Finite-dimensional separation
gives a nonzero separating vector with nonnegative coordinates: a negative
coordinate would make its infimum on that upward-unbounded orthant equal
to minus infinity. Normalize its coordinate sum to one. The infimum of
its pairing over the open orthant is then beta. Separation gives exactly
(11). Conversely, (11) makes the pi-weighted average of the row payoffs
at any lambda at most beta, so not every row payoff can exceed beta.
This proves both directions, including equality cases.

Applying the same argument at beta=tau gives the full finite minimax
identity

    tau=min_(pi>=0,sum pi=1) max_v sum_p pi_p A_(p,v).

At an unrestricted local depth minimum, (11) must therefore hold for
EVERY selected critical circuit at each deepest base and EVERY finite
exposed-vertex set with its chosen exposing functionals, whenever the
equal-slope hypothesis holds. The probability pi may depend on this
selection. It is not one fixed stress asserted for all circuits.

This is stronger than separate pointwise protection. The latter only
says each column has some entry <=beta. A convex combination of columns
can have ALL entries greater than beta, and (11) is precisely the
obstruction to that happening. It is an incidence condition at original
vertices, not a bound on compatibility repair costs.

### 4.1 A sharp support bound for a profitable trim distribution

An optimizer in (9) can be chosen with support at most k, the number of
deepest bases. Choose an optimizer of minimal support and a dual optimizer
pi at tau. Equality of primal and dual values forces every positively
weighted column to satisfy pi.A_(.,v)=tau. Thus the vectors
(1,A_(.,v)) on that support lie in a linear subspace of dimension at most
k: the nonzero relation pi.A−tau*1=0 holds on them. If more than k were
present, a nonzero linear dependence would preserve both the sum of
weights and every row payoff. Its coefficients have both signs, and
moving along it until one weight first vanishes reduces support while
preserving optimality, a contradiction.

Accordingly, if this smooth-incidence mechanism succeeds, at most k
disjoint vertex trims suffice. No bound k<=2^n is assumed.

## 5. A complete example defeating every single-point trim obstruction

Fix n>=2,d>=2, put L=2^(n−1), and let Q_d=[−1,1]^d have volume w=2^d.
Start with

    C=[−1,1]×[0,1]^(n−1)×Q_d.

As proved in the preceding note, its maximum depth is beta=1/(2L)=2^(−n).
Its deepest integer bases are (0,eta), eta in {0,1}^(n−1), at continuous
center zero. Every fiber has mass w<M/2^n=3w/2. Every sufficiently small
trim at ONE ambient exposed point strictly increases maximum depth,
because a different binary layer remains unchanged at absolute depth

    q=3w/2.

In fact a single deletion of mass epsilon has exact new depth
q/(2qL−epsilon): the unchanged layer supplies this lower bound, while
the original layer-isolating median-cap covers retain masses at most q
after deletion and supply the matching upper bound.

Choose one exposed vertex v_eta=(1,eta,1,...,1) per binary layer. It is
exposed by

    ell_eta(z,k,x)=z+sum_i(2 eta_i−1)k_i+sum_j x_j.

Its support value is 1+sum_i eta_i+d. For 0<t<=1, moving that support
value inward by t changes just the fiber (1,eta), removing the simplex
sum_j(1−x_j)<t, of volume

    delta=t^d/d!.

All other integer bases have support gap at least one. The L simultaneous
inequalities therefore remove disjoint equal masses delta, exactly one
from each binary layer, preserving all actual fibers and compatibility.
The total removed mass is epsilon=L delta.

At each deepest base use the three critical continuous normals

    (1,0,...), (0,1,0,...), (−1,−1,0,...)/sqrt(2)

with weights (1,1,sqrt(2)). A sufficiently large fixed integer tilt in
the binary coordinates excludes every other eta-layer for each cap,
without changing its restriction in its own layer. Its continuous section
areas there are q,q,sqrt(2)q, so all reciprocal-section probabilities are
1/3. All cuts are proper in the three own-layer fibers, and all other
layers are strictly excluded; the equal-slope hypothesis holds.

At v_eta the first two caps of its own circuit have incidence one and
the third zero. All other layer circuits have incidence zero. Thus

    A=(2/3) identity_L,       tau=2/(3L)>1/(2L)=beta.      (12)

Uniform lambda_eta=1/L attains this value. Any single-column distribution
has minimum payoff zero. In fact every profitable distribution for this
matrix must use ALL L vertices, so the support bound in Section 4.1 is
sharp. This provides an actual geometric separation between pointwise
protection and simultaneous-distribution protection.

There is also a finite exact all-candidate certificate, independent of
the asymptotic argument. In each binary layer use the three caps

    x_1>=−delta/(3q),
    x_2>=−delta/(3q),
    x_1+x_2<=−2delta/(3q),

with the same sufficiently large fixed tilts excluding other layers.
They cover its entire continuous plane at every z; their weighted margins
sum to zero. The deleted simplex is wholly in the first two caps and
disjoint from the third because t<=1. In the affected layer their masses
are exactly

    q−2delta/3,
    q−2delta/3,
    q−2delta/3+delta²/(9q).                              (13)

For the first two, a threshold displacement adds delta/3 to the cap mass
of the three unchanged boxes, after which delta is deleted. For the third,
the square sum-section formula, multiplied by 3·2^(d−2), is
q−q h+q h²/4 at h=2delta/(3q). The upper corner deletion is disjoint.
The complete source mass is L(2q−delta). Its full maximum depth therefore
satisfies

    D_new <= [q−2delta/3+delta²/(9q)]/[L(2q−delta)]
      =1/(2L)−delta(3q−2delta)/[18qL(2q−delta)] <1/(2L).  (14)

Every cap remains an actual finite ambient halfspace, and these circuits
cover all candidates in all new fibers. No selected-center lower bound
is being substituted for the maximum. The new source still has no heavy
fiber: its largest mass w is below (3w−delta)/2=M_new/2^n because
delta<w. Formula (14) concerns a source above the OC target; it proves no
below-target descent theorem.

## 6. Dimension one and the scope of the incidence simplification

Construction (2), exact prescribed masses, and exact quantile covers work
also for d=1. If every selected cap avoids every trimmed vertex, the
moving-threshold/removal interaction is zero for small epsilon, and
Sections 3--4 remain valid with their stated threshold slopes.

If a selected cap passes through a trimmed endpoint in d=1, the interaction
need not be lower order. There is instead an exact endpoint inverse rule.
Each fiber is an interval. Give every endpoint its outward velocity r_F:
r_F=−lambda_v for its selected vertex, and zero if it is not trimmed.
For a cap whose threshold also moves by epsilon s, its first mass
coefficient is

    f_j(lambda,s)=
       sum_(endpoints strictly inside H_j) r_F
       −S_(proper,j) s
       +sum_(coincident inside endpoints) min(r_F,−s)
       +sum_(coincident outside endpoints) max(r_F−s,0).  (15)

Each proper interval section has H_0 mass one; supporting coincidences
use the actual endpoint min/max rules. The anchor's proper section makes
f_j strictly decreasing onto R as a function of s. Its inverse in s is
therefore well defined. For a circuit there is a unique common budget
coefficient a_C satisfying

    sum_j rho_j f_j(lambda,.)^(-1)(a_C)=0.                (16)

The corresponding threshold velocities give an exact whole-fiber cover.
If a_C<−beta for one selected circuit at EVERY deepest base, the full
maximum depth decreases. Formula (15) follows directly by comparing the
moving interval endpoint and moving cap threshold, so it retains every
boundary interaction. Its piecewise-linear inverse is the archived exact
quantile rule specialized to the actual simultaneous endpoint deletions.
The simple matrix dual is not asserted when those endpoint interactions
are present.

## 7. Remaining numerical issue

The new necessary invariant is the finite dual (11), universally over
critical circuit selections and feasible exposed-vertex deletion patterns;
the nonsmooth version is (7). It is strictly stronger than separate
single-point protection and has the explicit realization (12)--(14).
It has not been proved that beta below Gamma_d/h(P), or below the OC
threshold, makes one such incidence game profitable. Vertex exposure,
cap incidences, section slopes, and the choice of critical circuits remain
coupled geometric data. No arbitrary-face classification or discarded
active base is being used to bypass that problem.

For calibration, take the sharp source {0,1}^n×T_d and its strictly
layer-isolating canonical simplex circuits. There are L=2^n deepest
bases. Their reciprocal-section probabilities are 1/(d+1), and every
continuous simplex vertex belongs to exactly one own-layer canonical
cap. The corresponding vertex game has

    tau=1/[L(d+1)] < Gamma_d/L=beta       for d>=2.

Thus the game is not asserted to recover the sharp constant merely by
counting vertices or normalizing one arbitrary critical cover. At a
hypothetical below-target minimum, the required contradiction would have
to use additional geometry to violate its universal dual protection.

## 8. Exact verification

`../assets/pk-nov6/computations/verify_simultaneous_vertex_mass_trims.py` independently constructs the
actual planar integer fibers by intersecting all exposing halfplanes,
then clips every original ambient cap at every integer base. It verifies
the exact masses in (13), the full decrement (14), and the no-heavy
inequality. It also checks the all-dimensional formulas and independently
enumerates rational primal and dual game vertices, including the support
bound. Output:

    PASS: 20 actual multi-plane source/cap certificates;
    324 all-dimensional strict-decrement/no-heavy identities;
    128 exact primal-dual/support game checks.

The proof of the construction and finite dual is uniform; these finite
checks are regression certificates for the explicit formulas.
